V01-K-001: Washing machines, vacuum cleaners and electric irons were sold to households with the promise that they would free people from the drudgery of domestic work. Yet many historians of the household have argued that the hours spent on housework fell far less than the advertisements implied. The explanation is that the machines did make each task easier, but they also raised the standard of what counted as done: clothes were washed after one wearing, and floors were expected to shine. The effort saved on each task was thus spent on doing more tasks more often, which is how a labour-saving device can fail to save labour at all.
V01-K-002: Few attachments are as durable as the one a person forms with a sports club in childhood. Players come and go, owners sell up, and the team may even move its ground to another part of the city. Through all these changes the fan's loyalty often survives, attaching itself to the name and colours rather than to any particular people. In this sense supporters are loyal less to a team than to a story about themselves that the team allows them to keep telling.
V01-K-003: No industry promotes given names, and nobody profits when a particular one becomes popular. Yet the popularity of a name rises and falls on the familiar curve of a fad, climbing slowly, peaking and fading within a generation, as though someone were marketing it. The puzzle dissolves once we notice how parents tend to choose: they look for a name that is uncommon but not strange, one that sounds fresh to their ear. Because parents of the same generation have heard much the same names while growing up, their ears agree, and they arrive independently at the same few choices. A name picked for its distinctiveness thus becomes common, and in becoming common it begins to sound dated to the next cohort of parents, who avoid it for the very reason it was once chosen.
V01-K-004: Open-plan offices were championed on the grounds that removing walls would encourage colleagues to talk to one another and share ideas. In many offices that adopted them, however, the effect has often seemed to be the reverse, as people put on headphones and send messages to colleagues a few desks away. Being visible to everyone, it appears, makes people more guarded rather than more open, since any conversation can be overheard by the whole room. Privacy, on this view, is not the enemy of collaboration but one of its conditions, because people share half-formed ideas only where they can afford to be wrong in front of a few listeners.
V01-K-005: Before mechanical refrigeration, ice was a harvested crop, cut in blocks from frozen lakes and ponds during the coldest weeks of winter. Packed in sawdust and stored in thick-walled ice houses, these blocks could last well into the following summer. Some merchants realised that well-insulated ice could survive even a long sea voyage, and began shipping it to hot ports far from any frozen lake. The trade collapsed only when machines that could make ice anywhere, at any time, removed the advantage of a cold winter.
V01-K-006: In several European cities of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, coffeehouses became places where strangers could sit together and discuss the news. For the price of a cup, a customer could read the pamphlets and newspapers left on the tables and join whatever argument was under way. What made these rooms unusual, however, was not the drink or the reading matter but the convention that rank mattered less inside them than the force of what one said. Some historians have seen in this convention an early form of public opinion, formed through argument among private persons rather than handed down by authority. Others caution that the openness was partial, since the customers were mostly men of some means, and the ideal of equal debate was more often professed than practised.
V01-K-007: It is tempting to suppose that writing was invented to record what people wished to say: their stories, their laws and their prayers. The earliest surviving tablets from Mesopotamia, however, consist overwhelmingly of lists of goods, rations and debts kept by administrators. On one influential account, these marks descend from small clay tokens that stood for quantities of grain or livestock long before anyone thought of representing a spoken word. If so, writing began not as a way of capturing language but as a way of keeping count, and only gradually acquired the power to say whatever a speaker could.
V01-K-008: Before postal reform in the nineteenth century, letters in Britain were usually paid for by the recipient, at a rate that depended on distance and the number of sheets. The system invited evasion: a sender could, for instance, mark the outside of a letter with an agreed sign, and the recipient could read the message at a glance and refuse to pay. Charging a single low rate, paid in advance by the sender, removed both the motive for such tricks and the labour of calculating each fee. The adhesive stamp was simply the device that made prepayment convenient; the real innovation was the change in who paid and how much.
V01-K-009: For centuries most European wars were fought by professionals and hired troops, while ordinary subjects contributed their taxes rather than their lives. When states began to require military service from the whole adult male population, they were asking for something far greater than money. Men compelled to risk death for a nation found it natural to ask why they should have no voice in how that nation was governed. Such demands for a voice shaped political debate in several countries, where the extension of the vote was argued for, at least in part, as the fair return for a burden every citizen now shared. If this reading is right, the right to vote and the duty to serve grew up together, and modern citizenship owes something to the barracks as well as to the debating chamber.
V01-K-010: Paying workers by the piece rather than by the hour seems an obvious way to reward effort, since those who produce more will earn more. And so it is, wherever output is easy to count and quality easy to see, as when fruit is picked and paid for by the crate. In tasks where a careless item looks much like a careful one, however, the same incentive rewards haste, and the employer ends up paying for work that must later be redone. The choice between the two forms of pay therefore turns less on how hard people are willing to work than on what the employer is able to measure.
V01-K-011: A lender advancing small sums to poor households faces two problems at once: it cannot tell careful borrowers from careless ones, and it has nothing to seize when a loan goes bad. Lending to small groups whose members are jointly liable for one another's debts addresses both problems without any new information ever reaching the lender. A member who must answer for a partner's default will choose partners known to be reliable, and will press any partner who begins to fall behind with repayments. By choosing and pressing their partners in this way, the members in effect do the screening and the collecting that the lender cannot, using knowledge no loan officer could gather cheaply.
V01-K-012: Many household goods, from phones to printers, seem to wear out or become unusable sooner than their materials alone would require. Critics call this planned obsolescence and accuse manufacturers of designing products to fail so that customers will have to buy again. Manufacturers reply that buyers themselves demand lighter, cheaper and more elaborate goods, and that such goods are inevitably harder to make durable. The truth probably lies between these positions, since both the design of products and the preferences of buyers shape how long things last.
V01-K-013: Supermarket loyalty cards are usually presented as a reward to customers, a small discount in return for coming back. For the retailer, however, the discount is less a gift than a payment, the price at which it buys a detailed record of what each household purchases. Such records reveal patterns that no shop assistant could notice, such as which products tend to be bought together and how a family's habits change over a year. With knowledge of such patterns the retailer can decide what to stock, where to place it on the shelves and which offers to send to which customers. Measured against the gains from stocking, shelving and targeting offers with such precision, the discount that pays for the information begins to look small.
V01-K-014: For much of the twentieth century, forest managers in several countries treated every wildfire as an enemy to be put out as quickly as possible. In forests adapted to frequent low fires, this policy allowed dead wood and undergrowth to build up year after year. When a fire eventually escaped control, it found so much fuel that it burned far hotter than the small fires it replaced, killing trees that would once have survived. Many managers now set controlled burns on purpose, accepting small fires in order to prevent catastrophic ones.
V01-K-015: Many vaccines lose their potency if they become too warm, and some are also damaged by freezing. They must therefore be kept within a narrow range of temperatures all the way from the factory to the moment of injection. This unbroken sequence of refrigerators, insulated boxes and cooled vehicles is known as the cold chain. In remote areas with unreliable electricity, keeping the cold chain intact can be harder than obtaining the vaccine itself, which is why heat-stable vaccines are so valued.
V01-K-016: Rivers fed by mountain glaciers are especially valuable in late summer, when rain is scarce and the ice releases water stored over many winters. As the climate warms these glaciers melt faster, and for a time the rivers they feed may actually carry more water than before. The extra flow comes from drawing down the store itself, much as a household might live comfortably for a while by spending its savings. Once the glaciers have shrunk past a certain point, summer flows must fall, and communities that planned around the temporary surplus will face a shortage they did not see coming.
V01-K-017: Along many tropical coasts, mangrove forests grow in the shallow zone where land meets sea. Their roots, arching down into the mud, break the force of waves and hold silt in place that the tide would otherwise carry off. For this reason, coastal villages behind healthy mangroves tend to suffer less damage from storm surges than villages on cleared shores. Yet mangroves have often been cut down to make room for fish ponds, ports and holiday resorts, which offer quicker returns. Some coastal authorities now replant them, having learned that the cheapest sea wall may be the one that grows by itself.
V01-K-018: Irrigation can turn dry land into some of the most productive farmland in the world, at least for a while. The water brought to the fields, however, carries small amounts of dissolved salt, which stays behind in the soil when the water evaporates. Over decades these deposits accumulate, and in poorly drained fields they can reach levels that stunt or kill crops. The very practice that made the desert bloom can thus, without careful drainage, slowly return it to desert.
V01-K-019: Many websites ask visitors to prove that they are human by reading distorted letters or picking out traffic lights in a grid of photographs. These tests rest on the assumption that some tasks are easy for people but hard for computers. As image-recognition software improves, however, the set of such tasks keeps shrinking, and the puzzles must grow harder to stay ahead. The odd result is that a test designed to admit humans and exclude machines increasingly frustrates the humans, while capable software often passes it.
V01-K-020: Every satellite launched into low orbit adds to a population of objects that will remain there, in many cases, for years or decades. When two such objects collide, they do not simply vanish but shatter into thousands of fragments travelling at enormous speeds. A fragment no larger than a coin can disable a satellite, and a disabled satellite struck again becomes a fresh source of fragments. Beyond a certain density, then, collisions could feed on themselves, multiplying debris faster than it falls back to Earth. Because of this tipping point, the danger does not grow in step with the number of objects in orbit, which is why a modest rise in launches may matter far more than it seems.
V01-K-021: In many new cars, physical buttons and knobs have been replaced by a single large touchscreen. Manufacturers favour the change because one screen is cheaper to build than dozens of separate controls and can be updated with new features. Drivers, however, cannot find a spot on a smooth screen by touch, so they must take their eyes off the road to adjust even the temperature. For this reason some carmakers have begun to bring back physical controls for the functions that drivers use most often.
V01-K-022: Studios favour sequels because an audience that enjoyed the first film is a market that already exists. The familiarity that guarantees this audience also sets a trap, since viewers want both to recognise what they loved and to be surprised. Lean too far toward the first desire and the film is dismissed as a copy; lean toward the second and it is accused of betraying the original. The best sequels escape this bind by keeping the characters audiences care about and placing them in a situation the first film never imagined.
V01-K-023: Theatre audiences are often said to watch a play through a 'fourth wall', an imaginary barrier that keeps the characters from seeing the people who look at them. An actor who turns to address those people directly is therefore described as breaking the wall, and the device is usually called modern and disruptive. Yet direct address is far older than the convention it supposedly breaks, since actors in many earlier theatres delivered asides and soliloquies straight to the crowd. What is modern, then, is not the broken wall but the wall itself, a convention that became dominant only when realism made the stage resemble a room with one side removed.
V01-K-024: Sampling, the practice of building a new track from fragments of existing recordings, became central to several genres of popular music. In its early years, producers often borrowed drum breaks and vocal phrases freely, treating old records as raw material. Once courts in some countries held that even short samples could infringe copyright, record labels began to insist that every fragment be cleared and paid for. The fees made dense collages of dozens of samples prohibitively expensive, and producers turned instead to a few licensed loops or to replaying the parts themselves. The law, in other words, did not merely regulate a style of music; by pricing certain sounds out of reach, it changed what that style sounded like.
V01-K-025: The back cover of almost any new novel carries short words of praise from other writers. These blurbs are meant to reassure a browsing reader that the book is worth the risk of buying it. Readers have learned, however, that authors often praise friends, colleagues and writers who share their publisher. As a result, a blurb now tells a careful reader more about the author's connections than about the quality of the book.
